To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) welfare losses of facing high-order risk increase are not necessarily superadditive, (ii) welfare losses of merging risk increases are not necessarily supermultiplicative, and (iii) welfare losses of risk increase are not always superadditive, but are always supermultiplicative, when background risks are taken into account.

(i) the nth-order utility premiums are superadditive when background risks are ignored; (ii) they may be subadditive when background risk are taken into account; (iii) they are subadditive for all individuals who are risk averse with respect to mixed risks; and (iv) they are sub-additive for all individuals whose preferences are risk apportionable.

(i) the nth-order utility premiums are not superadditive in general; (ii) they are superadditive when risk aversion is mixed; (iii) they are super-additive when risk apportionment prevails; (iv) they are subadditive when risk apportions are negative and mixed aversion is not strong enough.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the welfare loss associated with facing a high-order risk is not only a function of the decision maker's risk attitude, but also of the background risk environment.
the welfare impact of merging changes in risks depends on whether background risks and their interactions are considered.
welfare losses of merging increases in risks are not always additive.
